content: In the past, progesterone was proposed as a potential treatment to prevent pre-eclampsia. Although it was not widely adopted in clinical practice for this purpose, recent hypotheses suggest that progesterone may play a role in fostering immunological tolerance between the fetus and the mother, potentially reducing the risk of pre-eclampsia. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of administering progesterone during pregnancy on the risk of pre-eclampsia and its associated complications. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register (as of January 31, 2011) and the metaRegister of Controlled Trials (as of June 2, 2010). The review included randomized trials that assessed the use of progesterone or other progestogens during pregnancy for the prevention of pre-eclampsia and its complications. Two independent reviewers evaluated the studies for inclusion and extracted the relevant data. Four trials involving a total of 1,445 women were included in the analysis. Three of these trials investigated the use of progesterone injections, while one trial examined the use of a progestogen vaginal gel. These interventions were compared to no progesterone treatment. The evidence from these trials was insufficient to demonstrate any significant differences between the progesterone and control groups in terms of the risk of pre-eclampsia (three trials, 1,277 women; risk ratio [RR] 1.25, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.95 to 1.63), fetal death (four trials, 2,594 babies; RR 1.34, 95% CI 0.78 to 2.31), preterm birth (three trials, 1,313 women; RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.10), small-for-gestational-age infants (one trial, 168 women; RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.19 to 3.57), or major congenital anomalies (three trials, 2,436 babies; one trial reported no events, and two trials reported RR 1.19, 95% CI 0.31 to 4.52). Additionally, no cases of masculinization of female infants were reported (one trial, 128 women). One trial provided long-term follow-up data for children, but these findings were excluded from the review due to significant loss to follow-up (54% at one year and 80% at 16 years). In one trial comparing progesterone injections to placebo, over 60% of women in both groups experienced side effects, which were generally mild and primarily localized to the injection site. In conclusion, the available evidence is insufficient to draw reliable conclusions regarding the effectiveness of progesterone in preventing pre-eclampsia and its complications. As a result, the use of progesterone for this purpose is not currently recommended in clinical practice.
